paras: The threatened lynching of Henry Mitchell Smith took place in Lexington, Kentucky, in August 1895, when a Black man jailed on a charge of assaulting a white woman near Payne Station was threatened by a crowd at the Fayette County jail. Wire dispatches carried in papers from Rhode Island to Utah predicted that he would be lynched, but county and circuit judges posted armed guards, no attack on the jail was reported, and Smith was sentenced in September to hang.

On the morning of Wednesday, August 14, a man entered the home of a woman living on Walter Payne's farm three miles from Lexington and, according to the reports, assaulted her. The first dispatches named her Mrs. Hutchings, the wife of a tobacco dealer; later ones named her Mrs. Mary Hudson, the wife of a prominent farmer, and one September report called her a widow.

Her screams brought men from a nearby tobacco field, and the man fled into a corn field that neighbors surrounded. County Judge Frank A. Bullock and Deputy Sheriffs Rogers and Bosworth went to the scene, and bloodhounds were sent for. An early wire said the man was surrounded by a posse and "will undoubtedly be lynched." A later dispatch that night said the hounds had tracked down a man named "Harp, alias Mud Danberand," caught at midnight, and that he would probably be lynched if the woman identified him.

From August 16 the jailed man was named Henry Mitchell Smith, held in the Fayette County jail on a felony charge since the night of the search. That day a railroad section hand, Jas. Hogan, and Molly Miller, "a colored woman," said they had seen Smith near the scene, and the Ledger reported that Mrs. Hudson's sons, Elijah and John, said they would come to the jail with 150 armed men and lynch him.

At 6 p.m. on Friday, August 16, Mrs. Hudson was brought into the city and identified Smith at the jail. Judge Bullock, joined by Circuit Judge Parker according to the Richmond Climax, ordered Deputy Jailer W. B. Wilkerson to summon fifteen armed guards, and the police chief placed special policemen on the streets leading to the jail. A large crowd gathered at the jail and stayed through the night, while word came that 100 to 150 armed men were assembling at Payne Station for a march on the jail; armed men in the city were said to be determined to prevent a lynching.

At 1:20 a.m. on August 17, two scouts returning from the neighborhood reported that people there had gone to bed and expected the law to take its course. Officials treated this as a possible ruse and planned to search everyone entering the courtroom for the examining trial that morning.

No report of a lynching attempt at the jail or courtroom appears in the coverage. In late September Smith was sentenced to hang for the assault; a Washington paper reported that Judge Parke set his execution, with that of George Green, for November 29.

Coverage came entirely from white papers, and the first wires ran under headlines that treated a lynching as certain, such as "WILL BE LYNCHED" in the Providence News and "Another Negro Who Will Be Lynched" in The Herald.

A Cincinnati Commercial-Gazette special describing the night at the jail was carried on August 17 in Indiana, West Virginia, Kansas, Missouri and Texas papers. Its headlines varied from "PROSPECTIVE LYNCHING" and "LYNCHING BEE IMMINENT" to the Wheeling Intelligencer's "A LYNCHING SEEMS INEVITABLE." Some desks openly took the crowd's side: the Fort Worth Gazette said the guards were sworn in "to Protect the Brute," and the Salt Lake Herald wrote that the crowd was "Determined to Lynch the Devil."
Kentucky papers gave the case brief, court-centered notices, such as the Climax's "Mrs. Hudson Identifies Smith" and the Ledger's "Sentenced to Death."

Reports differ on names: the woman appears as Mrs. Hutchings in the first dispatches and as Mrs. Mary Hudson in all later and court reports, and the man caught on the first night was named "Harp, alias Mud Danberand" before later dispatches called him Henry Mitchell Smith, without saying whether they were the same man.

accounts.label: Kentucky dispatches in the Maysville Ledger
accounts.gist: An unknown man entered Mrs. Hutchings's house on Walter Payne's farm and fled into a corn field that neighbors surrounded; two days later, two witnesses placed Henry Mitchell Smith near the scene and Mrs. Hudson's sons threatened to lynch him.

accounts.label: Commercial-Gazette special (Aug. 16-17)
accounts.gist: Mrs. Mary Hudson identified Smith at the jail; judges posted armed guards while a crowd waited for 100 to 150 armed men from Payne Station; by 1:20 a.m. scouts said the country people had gone to bed, which was thought a ruse.

accounts.label: Sentencing reports (September)
accounts.gist: Smith was sentenced to hang for assaulting Mrs. Hudson, with execution set for Nov. 29.

framing.detail: Early headlines announced a lynching as settled: 'WILL BE LYNCHED', 'Another Negro Who Will Be Lynched', 'A Negro to Be Lynched'.
The jail-siege dispatch called Smith a 'Negro Ravisher' and the crowd 'orderly, but determined on business', while reporting the judges' guard order and armed townsmen opposed to a lynching.
Western headline writers sided against the prisoner: the Fort Worth Gazette said the guards were 'Sworn in to Protect the Brute', and the Salt Lake Herald wrote 'Determined to Lynch the Devil'.
Kentucky papers ran short court-centered notes: 'Mrs. Hudson Identifies Smith', 'Sentenced to Death'.
